notes.meaning: God speaks to Moses again. The book seemed to end with chapter 26, so this chapter is like an extra section added at the end. It deals with vows, which are promises people chose to make to God. God did not require these promises, but He gave rules for them.

A "special vow" was an unusual promise. In it a person gave himself, or one of his children, to the LORD. Often this came from deep thankfulness, or from a prayer for help in trouble. Usually the person did not go to work at the tabernacle (the worship tent). Instead the person was "bought back" by paying a set price. That money went to the upkeep of God's house.

Grown men from twenty to sixty had the highest price, fifty shekels of silver. That was because they could do the most work. Women of the same age were set at thirty shekels. The "sanctuary shekel" was the standard, full-weight coin kept at God's house. Matthew Henry adds that these differences belong to the old law. In Christ there is neither male nor female.

Young people from five to twenty had lower prices, because they could not yet do as much work. Little children from one month to five years had the smallest prices. Parents could vow a child to God, even before the child was born, as Hannah did with Samuel. But the child was not valued until a month old.

People over sixty were valued less than adults in their prime, but more than small children. In old age the prices for men and women came closer together. An old Jewish saying grew from this: "An old woman in a house is a treasure in a house."

If the person who made the vow was too poor to pay, the priest set a lower price he could afford. Even the poor still paid something, so that no one made vows carelessly. But no one had to ruin his family to keep a vow. God asks of people according to what they have, not what they lack.

A clean animal, one fit for sacrifice, became holy once it was promised. That means it was set apart for God. The owner could not swap it for another animal, whether worse or even better. If he did swap, both animals belonged to God. This rule taught people to think before vowing and to stick to their word.

An unclean animal, such as a donkey, could not be offered on the altar. So it was brought to the priest, and he set a fair price on it. Then the priests could use it or sell it, and the money served God's house.

If the owner wanted his animal back, he paid the priest's price plus one fifth more. This extra amount made people think twice before vowing. It also made them careful before taking back what they had promised. For example, an animal valued at forty shekels cost the owner forty-eight to buy back.

A man could also give his house to God. The priest set its value, and the house could be sold for the good of the sanctuary. If the owner had second thoughts and wanted it back, he paid the value plus a fifth. Matthew Henry adds that we can make our homes holy to the LORD today when we and our households serve Him.

A man could give part of his family land to God, but not all of it. God would not let a man's zeal leave his family poor. The land was valued by how much barley seed it took to sow it. Fifty shekels was set for each homer of seed, a large measure. Many explain that this price covered the whole span of years until the Jubilee.

The Jubilee came every fiftieth year. In that year land went back to the family that first received it. If a field was given right after a Jubilee, the full price stood. If it was given later, the price went down for each year already passed, because fewer years were left.
The man who gave the field could buy it back by paying its value plus a fifth. Then the field was his again. The money went to the sanctuary.

If the man did not buy the field back, and it was sold to someone else, he lost the right to redeem it. At the Jubilee it did not return to him. It became the priests' land for good. This rule pushed families to redeem their inherited land so it would not leave the family.

Land a man had bought, rather than inherited, was handled differently. It truly belonged to him only until the Jubilee, when it went back to its first owner. So he gave God the value of those remaining years in money, paid that same day. God would not let a gift to Him cheat a neighbour out of his land.
All these prices were to use the standard shekel kept at the sanctuary. That shekel weighed twenty gerahs, a small unit of weight. A fixed standard kept every valuation fair and honest.

No one could vow a firstborn animal to God, because it already belonged to Him by law. Giving it would be like handing God what was already His and calling it a gift. A vow was meant to go beyond what a person already owed.

This verse covers the firstborn of an unclean animal, which could not be sacrificed. The owner could buy it back at the set price plus a fifth. If he did not, it was sold, and the money went to God's house.

Something "devoted" to the LORD was given in the most solemn way. Often the giver called a curse on himself if he broke his word. Such a thing could never be sold or bought back. It was "most holy," fully and forever God's.

This verse does not let a parent or master put a child or servant to death by a vow. Murder was forbidden. It means people already condemned by God's judgment, such as the Canaanite nations or Jericho, who could not buy their way out. Clarke stresses this was justice on the wicked, not a human sacrifice. Some think Jephthah misunderstood this law when he sacrificed his daughter.

A tithe means a tenth. A tenth of all crops and fruit belonged to the LORD. Tithing was older than this law, since Abraham and Jacob gave tenths. Giving it showed that God owned the land and gave its harvest, and that His people lived on it as His tenants. Matthew Henry adds that we are still taught to honor the Lord with our wealth and to support His ministers.

A man could pay money instead of giving part of his crop tithe. But he had to add a fifth to its value. This stopped people from trying to gain by the swap and cheating the Levites, the tribe that served at God's house.

Animals were counted one by one as they passed under the shepherd's rod, and every tenth one was the LORD's. The owner could not pick out good or bad ones or make swaps. If he swapped, both animals became holy. Animal tithes could not be bought back, so the Levites would not end up with only the poorest beasts.

This closing line wraps up the whole book. These laws came from God at Mount Sinai. Some were moral and always binding. Others were ceremonial, meaning rules for worship given to Israel in its time, and they point to Christ. Christians are not under these ceremonies. Still, they should serve God with no less care and give thanks for Jesus.

other.view: Because the book seems to end at chapter 26, some have suggested an editor moved this chapter here from an earlier place in the book.
